chapter.name: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
chapter.blurb: Everyday mixtures are separated by matching the method to a property difference: handpicking, threshing and winnowing (size/shape/weight); sieving (particle size); evaporation (a dissolved solid from a liquid); sedimentation, decantation and filtration (solids from a liquid); churning (butter from curd) and magnetic separation (magnetic from non-magnetic). Complex mixtures need several methods combined in a sensible order.

scope_in.item: Handpicking: picking unwanted particles by hand based on differences in size, colour or shape; convenient when the particles are few and easily picked

Threshing: beating harvested stalks to separate grains from them; winnowing: separating heavier grains from lighter husk using wind or blown air (e.g. a bamboo tray/soop); mechanical threshers do both together
Sieving: separating a solid-solid mixture whose components differ in particle size, using a sieve whose hole size matters (e.g. flour from bran, pebbles from sand)

Evaporation used to recover a solid dissolved in a liquid, e.g. obtaining common salt from seawater in shallow pits, or from a salt solution heated in a china dish; Sambhar Lake as an Indian salt source

Sedimentation (heavier insoluble solid settling at the bottom of a liquid) and decantation (pouring off the liquid on top without disturbing the settled solid); decantation does not fully remove all particles and is also used in washing rice/pulses
Filtration: passing a mixture through a material with pores (filter paper, cloth, cotton, charcoal, sand) so the liquid (filtrate) passes through and solid particles (residue) are retained
Churning: extracting butter (lighter, floats) from curd (buttermilk left behind), using a churner (mathni)

Magnetic separation: using a magnet to separate magnetic substances (e.g. iron) from non-magnetic substances in a mixture; used by recyclers, sometimes with magnets fitted to cranes, to recover scrap iron

Two general purposes of separating substances: to obtain two different but useful components, or to remove a component that is not useful; a mixture with more than two components generally needs a combination of several methods, in a sensible order

concepts.name: Handpicking, threshing and winnowing
concepts.description: Handpicking removes particles by hand; threshing beats grains free of stalks; winnowing uses wind to blow away lighter husk from heavier grain.
concepts.idea: Handpicking removes unwanted particles by hand based on differences in size, colour or shape; threshing beats harvested stalks to separate grains from them; winnowing uses wind or blown air to separate lighter husk from heavier grains.
concepts.rule: Handpicking works best when the unwanted particles are present in small quantities and can be easily picked out; winnowing works because blowing air carries away the lighter component while the heavier component falls close by.
concepts.example: Picking small stones out of rice by hand is handpicking; beating harvested wheat stalks on a wooden log to separate grains is threshing; using a bamboo tray to blow air through threshed grain and blow away the husk is winnowing.

concepts.name: Sieving
concepts.description: Sieving separates solid-solid mixtures whose components differ in particle size, letting smaller particles pass while larger ones stay on the sieve.
concepts.idea: Sieving separates the components of a solid-solid mixture that have different particle sizes, by letting smaller particles pass through the holes of a sieve while larger particles remain on top.
concepts.rule: Sieving only works if the sieve's holes are smaller than the larger particles but bigger than the smaller particles; if the holes are too large, no separation occurs.
concepts.example: Sifting flour through a sieve lets fine flour pass through while bran and small stones remain on the sieve; sieves also separate pebbles and stones from sand at construction sites.

concepts.name: Evaporation to separate a dissolved solid from a liquid
concepts.description: Evaporation removes the liquid from a solution as vapour, leaving a dissolved solid such as salt behind.
concepts.idea: When a solid is fully dissolved in a liquid to form a solution, evaporation can be used to get the solid back by letting the liquid evaporate away, leaving the solid behind.
concepts.rule: Common salt is obtained from seawater kept in shallow pits exposed to sunlight and air until the water evaporates completely; a salt solution heated in a china dish leaves solid salt behind once the water has boiled away.
concepts.example: A few drops of salt solution dried on dark paper leave visible salt patches once the water evaporates; heating a salt solution in a china dish until the water boils away leaves solid salt in the dish.

concepts.name: Sedimentation, decantation and filtration
concepts.description: A heavier solid settles by sedimentation, the liquid is poured off by decantation, and a filter catches remaining fine particles by filtration.
concepts.idea: Sedimentation is the settling of a heavier, insoluble solid at the bottom of a liquid; decantation is removing the liquid on top by careful pouring; filtration passes a mixture through a material with pores so liquid (filtrate) passes and solid (residue) is caught.
concepts.rule: Decantation alone does not completely separate all solid particles, since fine particles may still be carried along when pouring; filtration, using filter paper, cloth, cotton, charcoal or sand, removes even very fine particles more thoroughly.
concepts.example: Letting brewed tea stand so tea leaves settle (sedimentation), then carefully pouring off the tea (decantation); pouring muddy water through a filter-paper cone leaves mud as residue and clear water as filtrate.

concepts.name: Churning and magnetic separation
concepts.description: Churning extracts lighter butter that floats away from buttermilk; magnetic separation pulls out magnetic substances such as iron using a magnet.
concepts.idea: Churning is used to extract butter from curd, since lighter butter floats to the top while buttermilk is left behind; magnetic separation uses a magnet to separate magnetic substances from non-magnetic ones.
concepts.rule: A substance attracted to a magnet is called a magnetic substance (iron is a common example); magnetic separation is useful when a mixture contains a magnetic component mixed with a non-magnetic one.
concepts.example: Churning curd with a mathni separates butter from buttermilk; moving a magnet through a mixture of iron nails and sawdust picks out the iron nails; recyclers use magnets, sometimes on cranes, to pull scrap iron from waste heaps.

concepts.name: Why we separate substances; choosing methods for complex mixtures
concepts.description: Separation either recovers two useful components or removes an unwanted one; complex mixtures need several matched methods combined in a sensible order.
concepts.idea: We separate substances either to obtain two different but useful components, or to remove one component that is not useful; a mixture with more than two components usually needs a combination of several separation methods.
concepts.rule: To design a separation procedure, first identify a property (size, solubility, magnetism, weight) that lets you split off one component, then repeat with the remaining differences, choosing methods such as handpicking, sieving, evaporation, sedimentation/decantation, filtration, churning or magnetic separation as appropriate.
concepts.example: To separate iron nails, sand, black pepper, stones, common salt and water: use a magnet first for the nails, handpick the pepper and stones, filter remaining fine particles, then evaporate to recover the salt.
